---
title: "Validation with observed hourly temperature: CEAZA-Met network"
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", echo = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 9, fig.height = 6, dpi = 96,
                      out.width = "100%")
options(knitr.kable.NA = "-")
metrics <- read.csv("data/ceaza-metrics.csv")
per_station <- read.csv("data/ceaza-per-station.csv")
stations <- read.csv("data/ceaza-stations.csv", encoding = "UTF-8")
weights <- read.csv("data/ceaza-ensemble-weights.csv")
label <- c(average = "Average", modified_average = "Modified average",
           single_triangle = "Single triangle",
           double_triangle = "Double triangle", single_sine = "Single sine",
           double_sine = "Double sine", hourly_linvill = "Hourly (Linvill)",
           hourly_sine = "Hourly (sine)", sine = "Sine (daily)")
index_label <- c(gdd = "Degree-days (base 10 degC)",
                 ch = "Chilling hours (0-7.2 degC)", cu = "Utah chill units",
                 cp = "Chill portions (Dynamic)")
level_col <- c(daily = "#0B5563", monthly = "#E8702A",
               gridded = "#8E5BA8")
```

This page compares thermify estimates with indices computed from
**observed hourly air temperature** at 30 stations of the CEAZA-Met network
in north-central Chile. It is the first empirical validation of the package
(`vignette("validation")` describes the protocol).

Data: Centro de Estudios Avanzados en Zonas Áridas (CEAZA),
[www.ceazamet.cl](https://www.ceazamet.cl), 2026. The hourly records are not
redistributed; this page uses seasonal totals derived from them. Scripts:
`data-raw/validation-ceaza/`.

## Stations and design

* 30 of the 53 CEAZA-Met stations with an air temperature sensor have at
  least 5 complete heat and chill seasons: 29 in the Coquimbo region and 1 in
  Atacama, latitude 29.1-32.1 degrees S, elevation 7-2,543 m, 2004-2025.
* **Reference**: each index computed directly from the observed hourly
  series (hourly means, local standard time).
* **Estimates** at three levels of information:
  * **daily**: the station's own daily minimum and maximum, with each daily
    method and with the hourly reconstructions (Linvill, sine);
  * **monthly**: the station's monthly climatology, densified with
    `pchip_mp`;
  * **gridded**: the WorldClim 2.1 30" cell of the station (1970-2000).
* Seasons: heat 1 September - 30 April (264 seasons), chill 1 May -
  31 August (313 seasons). Seasons with a gap longer than 2 hours are
  excluded.

## Pooled results from daily extremes

```{r table-daily}
d <- metrics[metrics$level == "daily", ]
d$index <- factor(index_label[d$index], levels = index_label)
d <- d[order(d$index, abs(d$rel_bias)), ]
tab <- data.frame(Index = d$index, Method = label[d$method],
                  Seasons = d$n,
                  `Relative bias` = sprintf("%+.1f %%", d$rel_bias),
                  MAE = round(d$mae, 1), check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(tab, row.names = FALSE, caption = paste(
  "Bias and mean absolute error (MAE, in the units of each index) of the",
  "season total, pooled over 30 stations. Methods ordered by absolute bias",
  "within each index."))
```

* **Degree-days: every method overestimates.** The averaging method
  (+5.4 %) and the Linvill reconstruction (+6.0 %, lowest MAE) are the
  closest; the methods that assume a symmetric day (triangle +7.2 %, sine
  +8.4 %) overestimate more, and the modified average most (+12.2 %).
  Double and single variants differ by only about 0.03 percentage points
  over a season.
* **Chill: the Linvill reconstruction is clearly the best**: chilling hours
  +1.0 %, chill portions -4.3 %, Utah units -9.3 %, against -9 %, -16 % and
  -44 % with the sine.

Why degree-days are overestimated: in this semi-arid climate the night is
long and cool and the warm peak is short, so the daily mid-range
(T~min~ + T~max~) / 2 is above the true daily mean (by 0.9 degrees C at
Illapel). The synthetic experiment
([Degree-day methods compared on synthetic temperatures](gdd-synthetic.html))
assumed a less skewed day and did not reproduce this bias.

## Station by station

```{r per-station, fig.height = 6.5}
methods <- list(gdd = c("average", "hourly_linvill", "single_triangle",
                        "single_sine", "modified_average"),
                ch = c("hourly_linvill", "sine", "hourly_sine"),
                cu = c("hourly_linvill", "hourly_sine"),
                cp = c("hourly_linvill", "hourly_sine"))
op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 9, 2.5, 1))
for (ix in names(methods)) {
  ms <- rev(methods[[ix]])
  x <- per_station[per_station$index == ix & per_station$level == "daily", ]
  vals <- lapply(ms, function(m) x$rel_bias[x$method == m])
  lim <- range(unlist(vals), 0)
  lim <- pmax(pmin(lim, 60), -60)
  plot(NA, xlim = lim, ylim = c(0.5, length(ms) + 0.5), yaxt = "n",
       xlab = "Relative bias per station (%)", ylab = "",
       main = index_label[[ix]], bty = "n", cex.main = 0.95)
  rect(-5, 0.4, 5, length(ms) + 0.6, col = "grey94", border = NA)
  abline(v = 0, col = "grey40")
  axis(2, at = seq_along(ms), labels = label[ms], las = 1, tick = FALSE,
       cex.axis = 0.85)
  for (i in seq_along(ms)) {
    v <- vals[[i]]
    v <- pmax(pmin(v, 60), -60)
    points(v, jitter(rep(i, length(v)), amount = 0.12), pch = 21,
           bg = adjustcolor("#0B5563", 0.6), col = "white", cex = 1.1)
    segments(stats::median(v), i - 0.3, stats::median(v), i + 0.3,
             lwd = 3, col = "#E8702A")
  }
}
par(op)
```

Each point is one station (daily extremes); the orange bar is the median;
the grey band marks ±5 %. Values beyond ±60 % are drawn at the edge. A few
coastal stations accumulate very few chilling hours, so their relative
errors are large even when the absolute errors are small.

## Monthly climatologies and WorldClim

```{r levels, fig.height = 4.6}
sel <- list(gdd = "average", ch = "hourly_linvill", cu = "hourly_linvill",
            cp = "hourly_linvill")
mat <- sapply(names(sel), function(ix) {
  sapply(c("daily", "monthly", "gridded"), function(lv) {
    metrics$rel_bias[metrics$index == ix & metrics$level == lv &
                       metrics$method == sel[[ix]]]
  })
})
par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 1, 1))
bp <- barplot(mat, beside = TRUE, col = level_col, border = NA,
              names.arg = c("Degree-days\n(average)",
                            "Chilling hours\n(Linvill)",
                            "Utah units\n(Linvill)",
                            "Chill portions\n(Linvill)"),
              ylab = "Relative bias of the season total (%)",
              ylim = range(mat, 0) * 1.15, las = 1)
abline(h = 0, col = "grey40")
legend("topleft", legend = c("Daily extremes", "Monthly climatology",
                             "WorldClim cell"),
       fill = level_col, border = NA, bty = "n")
```

* **Monthly climatologies lose the cold nights.** Densified monthly values
  have no day-to-day variability, so chilling hours are underestimated by
  about 25 %. Utah units are almost unbiased on average (-0.9 % with
  Linvill), but with a much larger error per season.
* **WorldClim cells are the least reliable here**, and the pooled bias
  hides two opposite errors (figure below). For chilling hours, the
  WorldClim cell gives **no chilling hours at all at 7 of the 8 stations
  below 200 m**, although some of them record 400-500 hours per season, and
  it **overestimates them 1.4 to 4.3 times at the 10 stations between 650
  and 1,700 m**.

```{r elevation, fig.height = 4.2}
g <- per_station[per_station$index == "ch" & per_station$level == "gridded" &
                   per_station$method == "sine", ]
g <- merge(g, stations, by = "station")
par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 1, 1))
plot(g$elevation, pmin(g$rel_bias, 200), pch = 21,
     bg = adjustcolor("#8E5BA8", 0.7), col = "white", cex = 1.3, las = 1,
     xlab = "Station elevation (m)",
     ylab = "Bias of WorldClim chilling hours (%)")
abline(h = 0, col = "grey40")
```

Each point is one station; values above 200 % are drawn at 200 %. The
pattern is consistent with cold-air drainage, which makes low valley
bottoms colder at night than an interpolated surface predicts, and with
warm thermal belts on mid-elevation slopes, but this analysis does not
prove it. The reference periods also differ (1970-2000 normals against
seasons of 2004-2025, a period of warming), and that effect is not
separated either.

## Ensembles

All daily degree-day methods overestimate at these stations, so the bias is
shared by every member. Stacking, Bayesian model averaging and Akaike
weights all put the whole weight on the averaging method, and the
cross-validated error equals that of the averaging method: **an ensemble
cannot remove a bias that all of its members share**.

```{r weights}
w <- weights[weights$weight > 0, c("scheme", "method", "weight", "cv_rmse",
                                   "cv_bias")]
w$method <- label[w$method]
names(w) <- c("Scheme", "Member with weight", "Weight",
              "CV RMSE (degC day)", "CV bias (degC day)")
knitr::kable(w, row.names = FALSE, digits = 3)
```

## What this means in practice

For semi-arid climates like north-central Chile:

* **Degree-days from daily extremes**: use the averaging method or the
  Linvill reconstruction (`gdd_methods = "hourly"` in `thermify()`), and
  expect an overestimate of about 5-6 %. Avoid the modified average except
  to reproduce a published convention.
* **Chill from daily extremes**: use the Linvill reconstruction
  (`hourly_method = "linvill"`, the default) and avoid the sine, especially
  for Utah units. Utah units and chill portions always use the hourly
  reconstruction. For chilling hours, `thermify()` and `thermify_rast()`
  count on the hourly reconstruction by default (`ch_methods = "hourly"`,
  since thermify 0.5.0); the analytical `ch_methods = "sine"`, the default
  in earlier versions, underestimates them (-9 % here).
* **Monthly climatologies**: chilling hours are underestimated by about a
  quarter; report them as approximate.
* **WorldClim**: treat values in mountainous terrain with great caution and,
  when possible, calibrate them with local stations.

## Limitations

* Arid and semi-arid sites only. The central-south of Chile (INIA
  agrometeorological network, Maule, Ñuble and O'Higgins) has not been
  validated yet, and the conclusions may change in more humid climates.
* Hourly means, not instantaneous or sub-hourly values, are the reference.
* One base temperature (10 degrees C), no upper threshold; season totals,
  not daily or weekly sums.
